cards.explanation: The answer is advance. Paul, who is writing this letter from his chains, says his circumstances “…have actually served to advance the gospel.” Chains, and he calls it progress. Most of us would send in a complaint. Paul sends in a progress report (Philippians 1:12).

The answer is the whole palace guard. Paul says, “…it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ.” The whole palace guard, friends. That news traveled farther than a rumor at a family reunion. And he says it reached everyone else too (Philippians 1:13).

The answer is False. Paul says most of the brothers are “…confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear.” So most of them weren't scared into silence. They were bolder, and I'd love to see that on a motivational poster (Philippians 1:14).

The answer is envy and rivalry. Paul says, “…some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.” So the same Christ gets preached from two very different places in the heart. It's like two cookie tables side by side at the same event, and one of them keeps counting the other's line. Paul doesn't hide it, he just names it (Philippians 1:15).

The answer is love. Paul says, “The latter do so in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel.” So these folks aren't just preaching, they're preaching in love. And they know what Paul is appointed to do. That's a good group to have in your corner (Philippians 1:16).

The answer is that they suppose they can add to the distress of his chains. Paul says the insincere preachers are “…supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains.” Notice the word supposing. That's what they think will happen, not what Paul says does happen. Paul's already in chains, and they figure they can pile something on top (Philippians 1:17).

The answer is True. Paul asks, “What then is the issue?” and then answers it himself: “Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached.” He cuts through all the drama like a man who's already done the math. What matters to him is that Christ is preached (Philippians 1:18).

The answer is rejoices. Paul says, “And in this I rejoice.” That's right after he admits some people preach with false motives. Most of us would be stewing in that situation. Paul looks at Christ being preached and picks joy (Philippians 1:18).

The answer is deliverance. Paul says, “…my distress will turn out for my deliverance.” Notice he says he knows it, not that he hopes it. That's a big statement from a man in chains. His distress doesn't get the last word (Philippians 1:19).

The answer is their prayers and the Spirit's provision. Paul says it will come “…through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ…” So the Philippians' prayers are part of this. And the Spirit's provision is right there next to them. Two things, side by side (Philippians 1:19).

The answer is False. Paul says he hopes “…now as always Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death.” That's both options, not just one. Either way, he wants Christ lifted up, friends (Philippians 1:20).

The answer is that he says he does not know. Paul asks, “So what shall I choose?” and then answers, “I do not know.” That's an honest answer. He says he is torn between the two. Paul doesn't pretend to have it all figured out (Philippians 1:22–23).

The answer is Christ. Paul says, “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.” Far better indeed, and he doesn't hold back on that. He's pointing at Christ as the reason (Philippians 1:23).

The answer is the Philippians. Paul says, “But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.” The "you" is the Philippians, the people he's writing to. So even though he calls departing far better, he keeps them in view. I think that's what a good friend does (Philippians 1:24).

The answer is True. Paul says, “Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith…” Back in verse 22 he said, “I do not know.” Now he says he knows. Keep up, friends (Philippians 1:22, 25).

The answer is to live in a way worthy of the gospel. Paul says, “Nevertheless, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ.” Then he says he wants to know they stand firm whether he comes and sees them or only hears about them in his absence. It's like doing good work whether the boss is watching or not. He wants their living to match the gospel either way (Philippians 1:27).

The answer is spirit. Paul wants to know they “…stand firm in one spirit, contending together as one for the faith of the gospel…” Think of a tug-of-war team, everybody pulling the same direction. That's the picture of contending together as one. And it starts with one spirit (Philippians 1:27).

The answer is the opponents' destruction and the Philippians' salvation. Paul says, “This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God.” The sign points both ways, one for the opponents and one for the Philippians. And Paul says it's from God. That's the text, and I'll leave it there (Philippians 1:28).

The answer is suffer. Paul says, “…it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him…” It's a heavy verse, and I think it's one to sit with for a moment. He puts believing and suffering in the same sentence. Paul doesn't dress it up (Philippians 1:29).

The answer is False, friends. Paul says, “…you are encountering the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.” They saw his struggle, and they hear he's still in it. It's the same one, so they share it (Philippians 1:30).
